Abstract.
This critical commentary outlines my contributions to knowledge over the last 23 years
of my career in developing the methodology of Therapeutic Coaching (TC), and its
application to fatigue related conditions such as ME/CFS, Fibromyalgia, Lyme Disease
and Long-COVID. Using the methodology of autoethnography, I have acted as both
the researcher and participant to explore the landscape within which I developed this
framework, and the key factors in bringing this work to an international audience of
millions of people. I begin with a selective literature review of the historical and current
mainstream treatments for fatigue related conditions, with a particular emphasis on
how these have been negatively received by patient communities. I go on to outline
the history behind the development of my clinic, the Optimum Health Clinic, and how
it found significant international success in creating a framework which addresses
some of these limitations. I then outline how I have used various online learning
mediums to reach a wider audience, in particular my Super Conference series which
has been attended by over two million people. This is followed by a chapter
introducing my professional training programs, which have trained hundreds of
clinicians in over 40 countries. I conclude with reflections upon the key learnings of
my career to date, and aspirations for the future, in particular a return to my academic
roots, which I hope this PhD will help facilitate.
Keywords: Therapeutic Coaching, Myalgic Encephalomyelitis, Chronic Fatigue
Syndrome, ME/CFS, Fibromyalgia, Lyme Disease, Long-Covid, fatigue related
conditions, autoethnography, online learning, professional training.

Chapter 1. Introduction.
1.1 Outline.
In this critical commentary, I aim to demonstrate that over the last twenty-three years,
I have made a significant contribution to knowledge which meets the requirements for
a PhD by Professional Practice. I will outline the personal and professional
experiences which have informed the development of Therapeutic Coaching® (TC),
an original and distinct therapeutic approach, which has had a significant impact in a
number of areas, most notably complex fatigue related conditions.
Using the methodology of autoethnography I will act as both the researcher and
participant in this study (Adams et al., 2015). I will utilise my publications, including
my first book WHY ME? which was autobiographical in nature (Howard, 2003),
recordings of my lectures and interviews, meeting agendas, emails, WhatsApp
messages, and conversations with colleagues. The aim is to take a deep dive into my
feelings, memories, and experiences over the years to allow me to better understand
the journey I have been on to develop the TC framework. My intention is to “truth
seek” into my development, to reactivate the key experiences that have shaped my
thinking, and to challenge my assumptions where possible.
My critical commentary will be comprised of the following six sections:
Chapter 1 – Introduction.
In this Introduction, I will outline my methodology and the use of autoethnography as
a research method (Adams et al., 2015; Bochner & Ellis, 2022; Carson & Niklasson,
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
2023; Heider, 1975). I will explain the reasons why I chose this method, the resources
I have at my disposal to work with, and why I feel particularly well placed to effectively
use this methodology. I will also consider the potential limitations of autoethnography
and acknowledge the inevitable bias of reporting on my own experience. I will then
move on to share a brief outline of my healing journey from ME/CFS (Howard, 2003)
and explain the personal context within which the framework of TC developed. I will
also offer a brief introduction to TC as a framework and the keyways in which it differs
from other therapeutic approaches. I will end the introduction with a summary of what
I believe to be my contributions to knowledge.
Chapter 2 – Selective literature review.
In Chapter 2, I will conduct a selective literature review to help further understand the
context within which TC developed. I will particularly focus on the lack of effective
treatments on offer for ME/CFS (Arron et al., 2024; Collin et al., 2012; Madison et al.,
2017), the alienation experienced by ME/CFS sufferers (McManimen et al., 2019;
Raine et al., 2004), and the controversy surrounding the PACE Trial and the use of
Cognitive Behaviour Therapy and Graded Exercise Therapy (Adamson et al., 2020;
Hughes & Tuller, 2021; Kindlon, 2017; White et al., 2011, 2013; Wilshire et al., 2018).
I will also touch on the relationship between ME/CFS and Long-COVID and how this
has impacted available support (Komaroff & Lipkin, 2023a; McKeever, 2024a). I will
then outline what I see as some promising areas for future research involving
mitochondrial function (Booth et al., 2012; Myhill et al., 2009; Tomas et al., 2019), and
Dr Robert Naviaux’s work on Cell Danger Response (Naviaux, 2014, 2023; Naviaux
et al., 2016). I will conclude the chapter with a brief introduction to the field of
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Integrative Medicine, including a note on my contributions to this emerging field (Bland,
2015; Howard & Arroll, 2011).
Chapter 3 – My development of effective clinical services.
In Chapter 3, I will outline my journey to build one of the UK’s most successful
integrative medicine clinics and how we have used TC to treat fatigue related
conditions. I will reflect upon some of the key inflexion points and what shaped my
key decisions. I will outline several elements of the TC model such as the ‘3 stages
of recovery,’ and the principle of ‘Bouncing the boundaries,’ which is an important
differentiation from Graded Exercise Therapy (GET) and Cognitive Behaviour Therapy
(CBT) (Howard, 2021). I will go on to share some of the difficulties of scaling an
effective clinical team and the challenging personal journey I faced in doing this. I will
conclude by considering the important role that developing our research base has
played in demonstrating the efficacy of our approach and the future work I believe we
must do in this area (Arroll, 2013a; Arroll et al., 2014; Arroll & Howard, 2012; Howard
& Arroll, 2011).
Chapter 4 – Creating some of the largest online events and programs in my
industry.
In Chapter 4, I will outline how I have utilised online learning and conferences to
popularise the TC approach and bring it to millions of people. I will share the story of
my first online program back in 2007, which involved a bi-weekly telephone conference
call with 250 live participants, and which was later the subject of a controlled trial (Arroll
et al., 2014). I will plot the course of my journey from these early beginnings to my
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
more recent ‘Super Conference’ series which has had over 2 million attendees,
including my hosting one of the biggest online health conferences in history, which
had 185,000 attendees during COVID-19. I will then focus on my most successful
online course, the RESET Program®, which has had over 7,000 students learning the
TC framework (Howard, 2023) and I will provide a brief module outline and explain the
logic behind this layout and structure. I will end with reflections on what I see as the
emerging future of online therapy and psychoeducation and the opportunities and
challenges I see within this.
Chapter 5 – Therapeutic Coaching professional training.
I will use Chapter 5 to introduce my professional training programs in TC and as an
opportunity to further introduce some of the key principles of the framework.
Professional training has been a critical element in both scaling the OHC and taking
the TC approach to many more people. These programs are now training hundreds
of new Therapeutic Coaches each year, and I hope to grow this into the thousands
per year. I will highlight one of my life ambitions, which is to make TC more widely
recognised and adopted than Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT). In this chapter, I
will also share some of my experiences building a successful YouTube channel
demonstrating the TC approach in action with real patients. This series has had over
3 million views and has been a fascinating process of balancing ethics and
safeguarding with ‘entertainment’ and creating a series which is engaging to watch.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Chapter 6 – Conclusion and contribution to knowledge.
In Chapter 6, I will summarise the key impacts on knowledge of my career to date and
reflect upon my experiences and learnings from the benefit of hindsight. I will share
the regrets of my career so far with regards to not staying closer to academia and
research, and comment upon why this PhD is an important personal step to address
this. I will also outline some of my ambitions and aims for the coming years. I will
conclude by making the case that I believe my impacts to date to be significant and
far-reaching and make my final arguments for my being worthy of a PhD by
Professional Practice.
1.2 Methodology – Autoethnography.
I have decided to use the research methodology of autoethnography for this critical
commentary. I believe this methodology is not only the best fit for the nature of this
project but also plays to my strengths as a researcher. In this section, I will briefly
outline the history of autoethnography, the method itself, and its criticisms, and
highlight why I believe I am well placed to use this method.
The Oxford English Dictionary defines ‘ethnography’ as, ‘The systematic study and
description of people, societies, and cultures.’ Autoethnography places the researcher
within the context of the research, as the investigator of the landscape they are
studying. Effectively, “cultural members give accounts about their culture” (Heider,
1975). Put simply, autoethnography invokes the self (auto), culture (ethno), and writing
(graphy) (Adams et al., 2015). Using this practice, the researcher is exploring their
inner landscape within the outer context of their relationships and environment.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
The first reference to the term ‘auto-ethnography’ is credited to Heider as a response
to the growth of identity politics and the recognition that not all circumstances are equal
in their capacity to conduct or engage in more traditional quantitative methods (Heider,
1975). Adams et al. make the point that “Not everyone has the time or technique, the
financial, physical, and social resources to write (White, male, upper-class) prose”
(Adams et al., 2015). By using an introspective method, to which the only barrier to
entry is the capacity to self-reflect, autoethnography allows researchers to explore the
experiences of a much larger number of people, making the research itself much
richer. Therefore, autoethnography not only serves as a helpful tool to investigate a
subject from the inside out, but it is also an effective leveller of engagement with the
process of research.
The steps of conducting autoethnography are (Cooper & Lilyea, 2022):

1. Establishing your research question.
2. Data collection.
3. Data analysis.
4. Synthesising the results of the data analysis.
5. Writing the autoethnographic report.
   I have followed these steps in writing this thesis, attempting to do so objectively and
   without bias.
   Autoethnography also provides a particularly useful method for a PhD by Professional
   Practice, as the very nature of the research is retrospective and self-reflective. In the
   case of this research project, some of the key events that have shaped my thinking
   ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
   happened nearly thirty years ago. However, that should not mean they are not
   relevant or important from the research perspective. The reality is quite the opposite:
   it is because of a number of these formative experiences that I have felt driven and
   compelled to focus my career in the ways that I have.
   One of the main criticisms of autoethnography is that it is too subjective and not real
   research. Adams et al. state that, “Some scholars critiqued autoethnography in simple
   ways, for example, referring to it as easy, narcissistic, unethical, and new, implying
   that it was unfamiliar or unrefined” (Adams et al., 2022). And yet, stories remain one
   of the most potent ways that human beings can impact each other, and one could take
   the perspective that we simply have not yet “Sanctioned storytelling and vulnerable,
   first-person, narration as an accepted academic genre of writing” (Bochner, 2012).
   Indeed, in my consideration of undertaking this PhD by Professional Practice, it was
   the moving autoethnographic account of my professor’s own doctoral journey which
   inspired me to take the leap (Carson & Niklasson, 2023).
   I was particularly drawn towards this research method for several reasons. Firstly, my
   undergraduate thesis used the qualitative method of Interpretative Phenomenological
   Analysis (IPA) and was later published in Psychology and Health (Arroll & Howard,
   2013). I enjoyed the process immensely. Indeed, this sparked a love of interviewing
   which has seen me interview hundreds of people over the last twenty years for online
   events. I was curious to allow myself to be the subject of such exploration in an
   academic context.
   ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
   Secondly, I had substantive source material to work with. I have previously written
   two autobiographical books. The first (Howard, 2003) chronicles my seven years
   suffering from ME/CFS. The second (which I chose not to publish, although much of
   the content is being used in subsequent books), chronicles an additional seven-year
   period of my trauma-healing journey. Together they account for fourteen of the last
   twenty-eight years of my life, with over 120,000 words. I have then shared extensively
   my personal experiences in my most recent two books (Howard, 2021, 2023).
   Furthermore, due to the online nature of much of my teaching, I have access to over
   300+ hours of recorded interviews, 200+ hours of my teachings, interviews, online
   courses, and 100+ hours of my filmed therapeutic work in my In Therapy YouTube
   series.
   The third reason why I feel autoethnography is the ideal choice is that it has many
   similarities to a key tool within the therapeutic TC framework this thesis is about,
   Therapeutic Inquiry. The practice of Therapeutic Inquiry involves either self-reflection
   on one’s own using journaling or speaking out loud, or in a small group of two or three
   people, where the subject explores the different layers of their inner experience, with
   the intention of increasing self-awareness and allowing inner movements to happen.
   This technique was inspired by my fifteen years as a student of the Diamond
   Approach, developed by Hameed Ali (penname A. H. Almaas). Almaas writes about
   the practice of inquiry extensively (Almaas, 2002, 2008), and as part of the thirty-five
   different week-long retreats I attended between 2001 and 2016, I undertook well over
   five hundred self-inquiries. Autoethnography has been described, “Not only as a
   method but as a way of life” (Bochner & Ellis, 2016) and I feel this is a life I have been
   living for many years.
